title: Supreme Court Questions Centre on Nuclear Accident Compensation Under SHANTI Act
excerpt: India's top court is examining whether the 2025 nuclear energy law's liability caps — set at Rs 3,000 crore for the largest plants — leave accident victims without adequate recourse, even as it signals reluctance to strike down the legislation.
body:
• The Supreme Court is hearing a PIL challenging India's SHANTI Act, 2025, which caps nuclear operator liability at Rs 3,000 crore — a fraction of cleanup costs from disasters like Fukushima ($180 billion) and Chernobyl
  • Chief Justice Surya Kant said the court's power to award compensation cannot be restricted by statutory caps, but called the challenge a "sensitive legislative policy issue"
  • Petitioners argue the Act exempts equipment suppliers from liability and weakens the regulatory independence of the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board
  • The case has been listed for further hearing, with the court promising to clarify key apprehensions about victim compensation

India's Supreme Court is pressing the central government on whether citizens can receive fair compensation in the event of a nuclear accident, as it examines a constitutional challenge to the SHANTI Act — the 2025 law that opened India's nuclear energy sector to private investment while capping operator liability.

A bench led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, alongside Justices Joymalya Bagchi and Vipul Pancholi, heard a public interest litigation filed by former civil servant EAS Sarma that challenges multiple provisions of the Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India (SHANTI) Act, according to Live Law and PTI.

The Liability Question

At the heart of the challenge is the Act's cap on nuclear accident liability. For the largest power plants, operator liability is limited to Rs 3,000 crore — approximately $319 million — while smaller facilities carry proportionately lower limits, according to the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists.

https://x.com/barandbench/status/2089246454598844543

Advocate Prashant Bhushan, representing the petitioners, told the court that the cap is "absurdly low" when measured against the actual cost of nuclear disasters. Cleanup costs from Japan's 2011 Fukushima accident have exceeded $180 billion, while the long-term economic consequences of the 1986 Chernobyl disaster run into hundreds of billions of dollars.

"Government can do whatever it wants by way of policy, but it cannot sacrifice Article 21 rights of citizens," Bhushan argued before the bench, according to Live Law.

"Our concern is that if an unfortunate event or any accident takes place and any person suffers an injury or damage, do we have a robust compensatory mechanism for that purpose."

— Chief Justice of India Surya Kant

Court's Balancing Act

The CJI acknowledged the gravity of the petitioners' concerns but signaled the court's reluctance to overturn what it characterized as a policy decision. "This is a very sensitive legislative policy issue," the bench observed, according to PTI.

However, the court made a key oral observation: the statutory cap on liability does not restrict a court's power to determine and award compensation to victims. "Nobody can curtail the power of even a tribunal when the tribunal wants to assess compensation and suitably award it to a person who is entitled," the CJI said.

Justice Bagchi added that when the state caps private liability through policy, "we are not here to second-guess decision making of the State in its subjective" assessment, according to Live Law.

The bench appeared to draw a distinction between challenging the constitutionality of the legislation and ensuring adequate compensatory mechanisms exist for victims — focusing its attention on the latter.

Supplier Liability and Regulatory Independence

Beyond the liability cap, the petition raises two additional concerns. The SHANTI Act eliminated the operator's right of recourse against equipment suppliers — a provision that had existed in the earlier Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act (CLNDA) of 2010, according to Bar and Bench.

Bhushan argued that exempting suppliers from liability could "encourage manufacturers and suppliers to cut corners in safety so as to maximise their profits." He pointed to the 1986 Oleum Gas Leakage case, where the Supreme Court established the principle of absolute liability for hazardous activities.

A Parliamentary committee reviewing the SHANTI Act separately flagged the supplier liability gap, recommending that "third-party independent auditing of supplier manufacturing sites" be made a statutory requirement, according to The Hindu Business Line.

The petition also questions the independence of the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB), arguing that provisions allowing government control over the appointment and removal of board members violate international conventions requiring regulatory independence from the executive, according to Live Law.

Comparing Global Standards

When the CJI asked Bhushan to name a country that had stopped using nuclear power, he cited Germany and Japan. Bhushan also noted that the liability cap in the United States is over Rs 1.54 lakh crore — more than 100 times the Indian cap — according to PTI.

India currently has 22 operational nuclear reactors and plans to expand capacity significantly. PM Modi announced a target of 100 GW of nuclear power by 2047 during his Independence Day speech on August 15, underscoring the government's commitment to nuclear energy expansion.

What's Next

The Supreme Court listed the matter for further hearing, promising to clarify some of the apprehensions raised by the petitioners. "Some of your apprehensions which require attention, we will try to clarify," the CJI told Bhushan, according to Live Law.

For NRIs with family members living near India's nuclear installations — from Kudankulam in Tamil Nadu to Jaitapur in Maharashtra — the case raises fundamental questions about safety governance, accountability, and whether India's nuclear ambitions are matched by protections for the people who live in their shadow.
nri_angle: Nuclear safety governance in India matters to NRIs with family members living near existing and planned nuclear installations across the country.
